question: A newborn presents with failure to thrive and very salty skin noted by the mother. Which of the following best explains the abnormal sweat composition?
cited_learning_objective: Outline the pathogenesis, clinical presentation, and pathologic changes of cystic fibrosis (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Defective CFTR chloride channel secretion
options.rationale: Correct: Mutant CFTR in sweat ducts fails to reabsorb Cl-, leaving NaCl on skin surface and producing salty sweat as described in the lecture.

options.text: Increased eccrine gland sodium secretion
options.rationale: Wrong: The lecture attributes saltiness to failed Cl- reabsorption via CFTR, not primary increased sodium secretion; this would be correct if CFTR-mediated Cl- reabsorption were intact but Na+ channels were upregulated independently.

options.text: Excessive aldosterone mediated retention
options.rationale: Wrong: Aldosterone causes sodium retention systemically, not hypertonic sweat; this would be correct if systemic mineralocorticoid excess produced concentrated sweat, which the lecture does not describe.

options.text: Primary eccrine gland structural atrophy
options.rationale: Wrong: Structural atrophy is not the mechanism in the lecture; this would be correct if glands were destroyed and only concentrated remnants remained, which is not taught.

options.text: Impaired aquaporin mediated water transport
options.rationale: Wrong: The lecture emphasizes ion channel defects (CFTR) rather than aquaporin dysfunction; this option would be correct if water channels, not ion channels, were primarily defective.

question: Which mutation class best describes a CFTR protein that is synthesized but misfolded and retained intracellularly?
cited_learning_objective: Outline the pathogenesis, clinical presentation, and pathologic changes of cystic fibrosis (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Class II abnormal folding and trafficking
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture states Class II (ΔF508) causes misfolding and ER retention of CFTR, preventing surface expression.

options.text: Class I defective protein synthesis entirely
options.rationale: Wrong: Class I causes absent protein due to synthesis defects; this would be correct if no CFTR protein were produced rather than misfolded.

options.text: Class III defective ATP gated regulation
options.rationale: Wrong: Class III affects channel regulation/function at the membrane, not folding; it would be correct if protein reached the surface but failed to open.

options.text: Class IV decreased channel conductance
options.rationale: Wrong: Class IV reduces conductance of surface CFTR; this would be correct if CFTR reached the membrane but had reduced ion flow.

options.text: Class V reduced protein abundance mildly
options.rationale: Wrong: Class V reduces quantity of CFTR but not folding retention; it would be correct if less protein were produced but properly folded.

question: A patient with recurrent sinopulmonary infections has thick dehydrated airway secretions. Which immediate ionic change in airway epithelium explains the viscous mucus?
cited_learning_objective: Outline the pathogenesis, clinical presentation, and pathologic changes of cystic fibrosis (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Decreased chloride secretion into lumen
options.rationale: Correct: Lecture explains defective CFTR reduces Cl- secretion, leading to increased Na+ absorption, water loss, and dehydrated mucus.

options.text: Increased bicarbonate secretion into lumen
options.rationale: Wrong: CFTR normally increases HCO3- secretion; increased HCO3- would hydrate and alkalinize secretions, opposite of lecture findings.

options.text: Primary potassium secretion into lumen
options.rationale: Wrong: Potassium handling is not the primary mechanism in the lecture; this would be correct only if K+ flux drove water movement, which is not described.

options.text: Enhanced chloride absorption from lumen
options.rationale: Wrong: The lecture describes decreased Cl- secretion, not increased absorption; this option would be correct if epithelial transport reversed direction in disease.

options.text: Increased aquaporin mediated water loss
options.rationale: Wrong: Water loss is secondary to ion shifts in the lecture, not primary aquaporin overactivity; this would be correct if water channels were pathologically upregulated.

question: Which clinical finding in infancy is most characteristic of intestinal obstruction due to thick meconium in affected neonates?
cited_learning_objective: Outline the pathogenesis, clinical presentation, and pathologic changes of cystic fibrosis (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Failure to pass meconium with distension
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture highlights meconium ileus presenting as failure to pass meconium and abdominal distension in newborns with CF.

options.text: Bilious vomiting without abdominal distension
options.rationale: Wrong: Bilious vomiting may occur but the classic sign is failure to pass meconium with distension; this would be correct if obstruction were high and early without distension.

options.text: Nonbilious vomiting and projectile emesis
options.rationale: Wrong: Nonbilious projectile vomiting suggests pyloric obstruction, not meconium ileus; it would be correct if obstruction were proximal to ampulla of Vater.

options.text: Passage of watery stools immediately after birth
options.rationale: Wrong: Watery stools are not typical of meconium ileus; this would be correct if there were diarrhea rather than obstructive meconium.

options.text: Jaundice with pale acholic stools
options.rationale: Wrong: Cholestatic jaundice is a liver manifestation, not the neonatal intestinal obstruction described; it would be correct if biliary obstruction predominated.

question: A patient with chronic productive cough has bronchiectasis on imaging. Which underlying cause is most commonly responsible for diffuse bronchiectasis in the United States?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the etiologies, gross findings, and clinical features of bronchiectasis (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Cystic fibrosis related airway obstruction
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture states CF is the leading cause of bronchiectasis in the USA due to thick mucus, infection, and airway wall destruction.

options.text: Postinfectious tuberculosis related damage
options.rationale: Wrong: Worldwide TB is the top cause, but in the USA postinfectious TB is less common; this would be correct in regions where TB predominates.

options.text: Primary ciliary dyskinesia causing retention
options.rationale: Wrong: PCD is a cause but less common than CF in the USA; it would be correct if the population had higher PCD prevalence.

options.text: Bronchial obstruction from endobronchial tumor
options.rationale: Wrong: Focal obstruction can cause localized bronchiectasis, not diffuse disease; this would be correct for focal, not diffuse, bronchiectasis.

options.text: Autoimmune mediated airway wall destruction
options.rationale: Wrong: Autoimmune diseases can contribute but are not the most common cause in the USA; this would be correct if systemic autoimmune disease were the predominant etiology.

question: Which structural change in bronchi is the hallmark gross pathology of bronchiectasis?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the etiologies, gross findings, and clinical features of bronchiectasis (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Irreversible dilation of bronchial airways
options.rationale: Correct: Lecture defines bronchiectasis as permanent dilation of bronchi due to destruction of supporting tissues from chronic infection and inflammation.

options.text: Concentric smooth muscle airway narrowing
options.rationale: Wrong: Concentric narrowing describes asthma or chronic bronchitis, not bronchiectasis; it would be correct if airway narrowing without dilation were present.

options.text: Diffuse alveolar septal thickening predominance
options.rationale: Wrong: Alveolar septal thickening is interstitial disease, not bronchial dilation; this would be correct for interstitial pneumonias rather than bronchiectasis.

options.text: Bronchial cartilage hyperplasia with rigidity
options.rationale: Wrong: Lecture notes destruction and sometimes ossification, not hyperplasia; this would be correct if cartilage overgrowth, not destruction, occurred.

options.text: Localized pleural effusion with adhesions
options.rationale: Wrong: Pleural adhesions can accompany severe disease but are not the hallmark bronchial dilation; this would be correct if pleural disease were primary.

question: A young adult with chronic sinusitis, bronchiectasis, and reversed organ placement is suspected to have a genetic motile cilia disorder. Which ultrastructural defect is most likely?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the pathogenesis and clinical presentation of Kartagener syndrome (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Absent or defective dynein arm proteins
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture explains PCD/Kartagener results from dynein arm defects causing immotile or dyskinetic cilia, leading to situs inversus and bronchiectasis.

options.text: Loss of peripheral microtubule doublets
options.rationale: Wrong: Peripheral doublet loss is less commonly emphasized; this would be correct if the primary defect were loss of doublets rather than dynein arms.

options.text: Central pair microtubule duplication anomaly
options.rationale: Wrong: Central pair defects can occur but lecture highlights dynein arm defects; this would be correct if central pair disruption were the dominant abnormality.

options.text: Basal body anchoring protein deficiency
options.rationale: Wrong: Basal body defects are not the primary mechanism discussed; this would be correct if ciliary anchoring, not dynein arms, were defective.

options.text: Excessive radial spoke protein expression
options.rationale: Wrong: Radial spoke overexpression is not described in the lecture; this would be correct only if radial spoke pathology caused immotility.

question: Which diagnostic test is most useful to confirm cystic fibrosis when newborn screening is positive but uncertain?
cited_learning_objective: Outline the pathogenesis, clinical presentation, and pathologic changes of cystic fibrosis (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Quantitative sweat chloride concentration test
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture lists the sweat test (pilocarpine-stimulated) with chloride thresholds as the confirmatory diagnostic test for CF.

options.text: Serum immunoreactive trypsinogen measurement
options.rationale: Wrong: IRT is used for newborn screening but requires confirmation by sweat testing; it would be correct only as an initial screen, not definitive.

options.text: High resolution chest computed tomography
options.rationale: Wrong: HRCT can show bronchiectasis but does not confirm CF; it would be correct if the question asked about pulmonary complications rather than diagnosis.

options.text: Nasal nitric oxide concentration measurement
options.rationale: Wrong: Nasal NO is used in PCD screening, not CF confirmation; it would be correct if evaluating primary ciliary dyskinesia instead.

options.text: Serum trypsinogen genetic sequencing panel
options.rationale: Wrong: Genetic testing of CFTR (not trypsinogen) can confirm CF; this would be correct if the option specified CFTR genotyping rather than trypsinogen sequencing.

question: A teenager with CF develops recurrent Pseudomonas aeruginosa lung infections. Which pathophysiologic change most directly predisposes to chronic colonization?
cited_learning_objective: Outline the pathogenesis, clinical presentation, and pathologic changes of cystic fibrosis (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Impaired mucociliary clearance from dehydrated mucus
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture emphasizes dehydrated, thick mucus due to defective CFTR leading to impaired mucociliary transport and chronic bacterial colonization like Pseudomonas.

options.text: Systemic immunoglobulin A deficiency alone
options.rationale: Wrong: IgA deficiency is not the primary mechanism in CF per the lecture; this would be correct if humoral immune deficiency were documented as the main defect.

options.text: Excessive alveolar macrophage activation
options.rationale: Wrong: Excess macrophage activation would tend to clear bacteria rather than predispose to colonization; this would be correct if macrophage dysfunction, not activation, were present.

options.text: Bronchial smooth muscle hyperplasia causing narrowing
options.rationale: Wrong: Smooth muscle hyperplasia is not the key predisposition described; this would be correct if fixed narrowing trapped secretions independent of mucus properties.

options.text: Primary ciliary beat frequency increase
options.rationale: Wrong: Increased ciliary beat would improve clearance; this would be correct only if ciliary hyperkinesis paradoxically impaired clearance, which is not taught.

question: Which clinical test is most helpful to screen for primary ciliary dyskinesia in a patient with chronic sinusitis and infertility?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the pathogenesis and clinical presentation of Kartagener syndrome (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Measurement of nasal nitric oxide production
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture notes very low nasal NO in PCD and presents it as a screening tool distinguishing PCD from other conditions.

options.text: Quantitative sweat chloride concentration test
options.rationale: Wrong: Sweat chloride screens for CF, not PCD; this would be correct if the suspected disorder were cystic fibrosis instead.

options.text: Serum alpha one antitrypsin level measurement
options.rationale: Wrong: A1AT testing evaluates emphysema risk, not ciliary dysfunction; this would be correct if emphysema due to A1AT deficiency were suspected.

options.text: High speed video microscopy of ciliary beat
options.rationale: Wrong: Although high-speed video microscopy can assess ciliary beat, the lecture highlights nasal NO as the screening test; this option would be correct as a confirmatory test rather than initial screen.

options.text: Pulmonary function testing with bronchodilator
options.rationale: Wrong: PFTs may show obstruction but are nonspecific; this would be correct only if the question asked about airflow limitation rather than ciliary dysfunction screening.

question: A patient with CF has fat malabsorption and steatorrhea. Which pancreatic pathologic change best explains these findings?
cited_learning_objective: Outline the pathogenesis, clinical presentation, and pathologic changes of cystic fibrosis (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Obstruction of pancreatic ducts with inspissated secretions
options.rationale: Correct: Lecture describes thick acidic secretions precipitating enzymes, obstructing ducts, causing exocrine atrophy and malabsorption.

options.text: Autoimmune destruction of islet beta cells
options.rationale: Wrong: Islet destruction causes diabetes, not primary exocrine insufficiency; this would be correct if endocrine, not exocrine, pancreas were targeted.

options.text: Diffuse pancreatic acinar hyperplasia increasing enzymes
options.rationale: Wrong: Hyperplasia would increase enzyme output, not cause malabsorption; this would be correct only if enzyme overproduction paradoxically impaired digestion.

options.text: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma causing obstruction
options.rationale: Wrong: Cancer can obstruct ducts but lecture attributes obstruction to thick secretions in CF; this would be correct if imaging showed a tumor causing ductal blockage.

options.text: Isolated loss of pancreatic endocrine function
options.rationale: Wrong: Endocrine loss causes glucose dysregulation, not steatorrhea; this would be correct if endocrine failure produced maldigestion indirectly, which is not described.

question: Which imaging modality is described as the diagnostic gold standard for confirming bronchiectasis?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the etiologies, gross findings, and clinical features of bronchiectasis (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: High resolution computed tomography scan
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture states HRCT is the hallmark diagnostic test for bronchiectasis, showing airway dilation and wall thickening.

options.text: Standard chest radiograph with lateral view
options.rationale: Wrong: Chest x-ray may show abnormalities but lacks sensitivity; this would be correct only if HRCT were unavailable and radiographic signs were definitive.

options.text: Bronchoscopic direct visualization of bronchi
options.rationale: Wrong: Bronchoscopy can inspect airways but is not the gold standard imaging modality; this would be correct if the question asked about endoscopic assessment rather than imaging.

options.text: Ventilation perfusion nuclear scan imaging
options.rationale: Wrong: V/Q scans assess perfusion/ventilation mismatch, not bronchial dilation; this would be correct if evaluating pulmonary embolism rather than bronchiectasis.

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the chest
options.rationale: Wrong: MRI is less commonly used and not cited as gold standard in the lecture; this would be correct if MRI resolution equaled HRCT for airway detail.

question: A 16-year-old with recurrent pneumonia and failure to thrive has sweat chloride 86 mmol/L. Which CFTR mutation mechanism most likely explains this presentation?
cited_learning_objective: Outline the pathogenesis, clinical presentation, and pathologic changes of cystic fibrosis (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Abnormal protein folding and trafficking defect
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture identifies ΔF508 (Class II) as causing misfolding and ER retention, the most common mutation leading to classic CF features.

options.text: Complete absence of CFTR protein synthesis
options.rationale: Wrong: Class I causes no protein synthesis; this would be correct if genetic lesion prevented translation entirely rather than misfolding.

options.text: Normal CFTR quantity with decreased conductance
options.rationale: Wrong: Class IV reduces conductance but lecture emphasizes folding/trafficking for common severe disease; this would be correct if CFTR reached membrane but had reduced ion flow.

options.text: Excessive CFTR mediated bicarbonate secretion
options.rationale: Wrong: CFTR loss decreases HCO3- secretion; this would be correct only if CFTR overactivity caused abnormal secretions, contrary to lecture.

options.text: Altered regulation of unrelated ion channels only
options.rationale: Wrong: Class VI affects regulation of other channels but is not the common ΔF508 mechanism; this would be correct if only regulatory interactions were disrupted.

question: Which reproductive consequence is most commonly associated with male patients who have the disease described in the lecture?
cited_learning_objective: Outline the pathogenesis, clinical presentation, and pathologic changes of cystic fibrosis (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Congenital bilateral absence of vas deferens
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture states ~95% of men with CF have CBAVD causing obstructive azoospermia and infertility.

options.text: Primary testicular failure with low testosterone
options.rationale: Wrong: CF causes obstructive infertility rather than primary testicular failure; this would be correct if endocrine testicular dysfunction were documented.

options.text: Retrograde ejaculation due to sphincter dysfunction
options.rationale: Wrong: Retrograde ejaculation is not the typical CF mechanism; this would be correct if autonomic sphincter dysfunction were the primary issue.

options.text: Sperm immotility from flagellar defects
options.rationale: Wrong: Sperm immotility is characteristic of PCD, not CF; this would be correct if the patient had primary ciliary dyskinesia instead.

options.text: Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism causing infertility
options.rationale: Wrong: Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism is not described in the lecture as a CF feature; this would be correct if pituitary dysfunction caused low gonadotropins.

question: A clinician considers CFTR modulator therapy that improves folding and trafficking of CFTR protein. For which mutation class is this approach most directly indicated?
cited_learning_objective: Outline the pathogenesis, clinical presentation, and pathologic changes of cystic fibrosis (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Class II misfolding and trafficking defects
options.rationale: Correct: Lecture notes lumacaftor corrects misfolding/trafficking (useful for ΔF508 Class II mutations) by improving transport to cell surface.

options.text: Class I absent protein synthesis defects
options.rationale: Wrong: Folding correctors require synthesized protein; this would be correct only if a therapy restored translation in Class I mutations.

options.text: Class IV decreased conductance channel defects
options.rationale: Wrong: Conductance defects are targeted by potentiators like ivacaftor, not folding correctors; this would be correct if the drug increased channel open probability.

options.text: Class V reduced abundance mild expression defects
options.rationale: Wrong: Reduced abundance might benefit from increased expression strategies, not primarily folding correctors; this would be correct if the drug increased protein synthesis.

options.text: Class III defective regulation by ATP gating
options.rationale: Wrong: Class III is a gating defect treated by potentiators; this would be correct only if the corrector also restored ATP regulation.

question: A patient with chronic productive foul-smelling sputum and hemoptysis has CT showing saccular bronchial dilations extending to pleura. Which histologic feature is expected?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the etiologies, gross findings, and clinical features of bronchiectasis (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Loss of cilia with chronic necrotizing inflammation
options.rationale: Correct: Lecture describes bronchiectasis histology with epithelial loss, necrotizing inflammation, fibrosis, and mucus plugging leading to dilated bronchi.

options.text: Noncaseating granulomas with multinucleated giant cells
options.rationale: Wrong: Granulomas suggest sarcoidosis or TB; this would be correct if granulomatous infection or disease were the primary process causing dilation.

options.text: Diffuse alveolar hyaline membrane formation
options.rationale: Wrong: Hyaline membranes are seen in ARDS, not bronchiectasis; this would be correct if acute diffuse alveolar damage were present.

options.text: Interstitial lymphocytic infiltrate with fibrosis
options.rationale: Wrong: Interstitial fibrosis describes interstitial lung disease, not the airway-centered necrotizing inflammation of bronchiectasis; this would be correct if parenchymal interstitial disease predominated.

options.text: Eosinophilic infiltration with bronchial hyperreactivity
options.rationale: Wrong: Eosinophilic inflammation is typical of asthma, not necrotizing bronchiectasis; this would be correct if allergic eosinophilic bronchitis were the cause.

question: A 4-week-old exclusively breastfed infant with prenatal paternal ΔF508 carrier status presents with lethargy and sunken fontanelle. Which electrolyte abnormality is most consistent with the lecture's salt-loss syndrome?
cited_learning_objective: Outline the pathogenesis, clinical presentation, and pathologic changes of cystic fibrosis (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Hyponatremia with hypovolemia and alkalosis
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture describes salt-loss syndrome in CF causing sodium loss in sweat, hyponatremia, hypovolemia, and chronic metabolic alkalosis, especially in hot environments or exclusive breastfeeding.

options.text: Hypernatremia with hypervolemia and acidosis
options.rationale: Wrong: Hypernatremia/hypervolemia is opposite of the lecture; this would be correct if excessive sodium intake or retention occurred instead of loss.

options.text: Hypokalemia with metabolic acidosis predominance
options.rationale: Wrong: The lecture emphasizes hyponatremia and alkalosis, not hypokalemic acidosis; this would be correct if renal tubular acidosis were present.

options.text: Hyperchloremia with normal sodium concentration
options.rationale: Wrong: Hyperchloremia with normal sodium is not the described pattern; this would be correct if chloride retention occurred independently of sodium loss.

options.text: Isolated hypomagnesemia without volume change
options.rationale: Wrong: Hypomagnesemia is not the salt-loss syndrome described; this would be correct if magnesium wasting were the primary defect.

question: A patient with chronic ear infections and hearing loss is found to have immotile sperm on semen analysis. Which additional finding would most strongly support a diagnosis of Kartagener syndrome?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the pathogenesis and clinical presentation of Kartagener syndrome (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Situs inversus with mirror image organ placement
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture describes Kartagener's triad—situs inversus, chronic sinusitis/bronchiectasis, and infertility due to ciliary dysfunction—so situs inversus strongly supports the diagnosis.

options.text: Elevated sweat chloride concentration on testing
options.rationale: Wrong: Elevated sweat chloride indicates CF, not PCD; this would be correct if CFTR dysfunction were present rather than dynein arm defects.

options.text: Alpha one antitrypsin deficiency genotype present
options.rationale: Wrong: A1AT deficiency causes panacinar emphysema, not ciliary immotility; this would be correct if protease inhibitor deficiency explained the pulmonary disease.

options.text: Diffuse interstitial lung fibrosis on imaging
options.rationale: Wrong: Interstitial fibrosis is not characteristic of Kartagener; this would be correct if the primary pathology were interstitial rather than airway-centered.

options.text: Congenital bilateral absence of vas deferens
options.rationale: Wrong: CBAVD is typical of CF-related male infertility, not PCD; this would be correct if CF were the underlying disorder.

question: A patient with bronchiectasis reports morning cough with large volumes of foul-smelling sputum that increases when changing position. Which physiologic explanation from the lecture best accounts for positional increase in expectoration?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the etiologies, gross findings, and clinical features of bronchiectasis (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Gravity mobilizes pooled secretions from dilated bronchi
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture notes dilated bronchi filled with pus and retained secretions; positional changes mobilize these secretions, increasing expectoration.

options.text: Positional bronchospasm increases mucus production
options.rationale: Wrong: Bronchospasm alters airflow but does not explain pooled pus mobilization; this would be correct if bronchospasm triggered acute mucus hypersecretion.

options.text: Diurnal cortisol variation reduces mucociliary clearance
options.rationale: Wrong: Cortisol rhythms are not discussed as a mechanism; this would be correct only if hormonal variation directly impaired clearance at night.

options.text: Postural venous congestion increases sputum viscosity
options.rationale: Wrong: Venous congestion does not account for foul-smelling pus in dilated bronchi; this would be correct if vascular congestion altered mucus composition.

options.text: Supine position decreases cough reflex sensitivity
options.rationale: Wrong: Decreased cough sensitivity would reduce expectoration, not increase it; this would be correct if positional suppression of cough were the primary factor.

question: A clinician orders nasal transepithelial potential difference testing for a patient with mild chronic cough and prior negative sweat test. The test shows a more negative potential than normal. Which epithelial transport change does this reflect?
cited_learning_objective: Outline the pathogenesis, clinical presentation, and pathologic changes of cystic fibrosis (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Increased sodium absorption across nasal epithelium
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture explains CF patients show increased Na+ absorption making the mucosal surface more negatively charged, increasing transepithelial potential difference.

options.text: Decreased chloride absorption from lumen to cell
options.rationale: Wrong: CF involves decreased Cl- secretion into lumen rather than decreased absorption; this would be correct if the primary defect were increased luminal Cl- removal.

options.text: Enhanced bicarbonate secretion alkalinizing surface
options.rationale: Wrong: CF decreases HCO3- secretion leading to acidic secretions; this would be correct if HCO3- secretion were paradoxically increased.

options.text: Primary potassium secretion causing depolarization
options.rationale: Wrong: Potassium flux is not the main determinant of nasal potential in CF per lecture; this would be correct if K+ movement dominated transepithelial voltage.

options.text: Loss of epithelial tight junction integrity increasing leak
options.rationale: Wrong: Tight junction leak would reduce potential difference, not increase negative charge; this would be correct if barrier disruption were the main abnormality.

question: A 6-year-old with recurrent otitis media and chronic cough has chest radiograph showing dextrocardia. Which embryologic process disrupted by ciliary dysfunction explains the organ laterality reversal?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the pathogenesis and clinical presentation of Kartagener syndrome (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Failure of nodal cilia to establish left right asymmetry
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture explains that motile cilia during embryogenesis determine left-right axis; dynein arm defects disrupt this, producing situs inversus.

options.text: Abnormal neural crest migration altering laterality
options.rationale: Wrong: Neural crest migration affects other structures but lecture attributes situs inversus to nodal cilia failure; this would be correct if neural crest defects caused organ reversal.

options.text: Defective somite segmentation changing organ position
options.rationale: Wrong: Somite segmentation affects vertebral patterning, not visceral laterality; this would be correct if somite anomalies repositioned organs.

options.text: Placental implantation site determining organ sidedness
options.rationale: Wrong: Placental site does not determine visceral laterality; this would be correct only in a hypothetical model linking implantation to organ orientation.

options.text: Abnormal left atrial morphogenesis shifting heart
options.rationale: Wrong: Left atrial morphogenesis is downstream of laterality cues; this would be correct if intrinsic cardiac morphogenesis, not ciliary signaling, were primary.

question: A patient with CF is started on ivacaftor. Which immediate molecular effect of this drug aligns with the lecture's description of its mechanism?
cited_learning_objective: Outline the pathogenesis, clinical presentation, and pathologic changes of cystic fibrosis (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Increases CFTR channel open probability at membrane
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture states ivacaftor is a potentiator that opens CFTR channels, enhancing chloride conductance when CFTR is present at the cell surface.

options.text: Enhances CFTR folding in endoplasmic reticulum
options.rationale: Wrong: Folding correction is the role of lumacaftor, not ivacaftor; this would be correct if the drug acted as a chaperone improving ER processing.

options.text: Blocks ENaC sodium absorption across epithelium
options.rationale: Wrong: Ivacaftor potentiates CFTR, not directly inhibit ENaC; this would be correct if the drug targeted sodium channels to reduce absorption.

options.text: Stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion directly
options.rationale: Wrong: Ivacaftor acts on CFTR channels, not directly on pancreatic enzyme secretion; this would be correct if the drug increased exocrine pancreatic output.

options.text: Inhibits bacterial biofilm formation in airways
options.rationale: Wrong: Ivacaftor's mechanism is ion channel potentiation, not antimicrobial; this would be correct if the drug had direct anti-Pseudomonas activity.

question: A patient with bronchiectasis develops massive hemoptysis. Which pathologic process described in the lecture most directly explains bleeding from dilated airways?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the etiologies, gross findings, and clinical features of bronchiectasis (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Erosion of bronchial mucosa with necrotizing inflammation
options.rationale: Correct: Lecture notes necrotizing inflammation and epithelial erosion in dilated bronchi, which can lead to hemoptysis, sometimes massive.

options.text: Pulmonary embolism causing infarcted lung tissue
options.rationale: Wrong: PE causes infarction and hemoptysis but lecture links hemoptysis in bronchiectasis to airway erosion; this would be correct if embolic infarction were the cause.

options.text: Left ventricular failure producing pulmonary edema
options.rationale: Wrong: Pulmonary edema causes pink frothy sputum, not massive hemoptysis from airway erosion; this would be correct if cardiac failure were primary.

options.text: Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage from vasculitis
options.rationale: Wrong: DAH is a separate cause of hemoptysis; this would be correct if systemic vasculitis caused capillary bleeding rather than bronchial erosion.

options.text: Bronchial artery aneurysm rupture unrelated to infection
options.rationale: Wrong: Bronchial artery rupture can cause massive hemoptysis but lecture emphasizes infection-related mucosal erosion; this would be correct if vascular aneurysm were documented.

question: A patient with suspected PCD has very low nasal NO and abnormal ciliary beat on high-speed video. Which long-term management strategy from the lecture is most appropriate?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the pathogenesis and clinical presentation of Kartagener syndrome (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Lifelong airway clearance and infection control
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture recommends airway clearance therapy and antibiotics for infections as lifelong supportive care for PCD since there is no cure.

options.text: Immediate lung transplantation as first line
options.rationale: Wrong: Transplant is reserved for end-stage disease; this would be correct only if irreversible respiratory failure unresponsive to supportive care were present.

options.text: High dose systemic corticosteroids indefinitely
options.rationale: Wrong: Chronic high-dose steroids are not the recommended primary management in the lecture; this would be correct if inflammatory control with steroids had proven long-term benefit.

options.text: Routine prophylactic antifungal therapy lifelong
options.rationale: Wrong: Antifungals are not standard lifelong therapy for PCD per lecture; this would be correct if fungal colonization were the dominant recurrent problem.

options.text: Gene therapy to correct dynein arm defect
options.rationale: Wrong: Gene therapy is not presented as an available treatment in the lecture; this would be correct if an approved gene correction therapy existed.

question: A patient with CF has fat soluble vitamin deficiencies. Which vitamin deficiency from the lecture is linked to squamous metaplasia of epithelial linings?
cited_learning_objective: Outline the pathogenesis, clinical presentation, and pathologic changes of cystic fibrosis (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Vitamin A deficiency causing squamous metaplasia
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture states vitamin A deficiency in CF can lead to squamous metaplasia of conjunctival, respiratory, urinary epithelia, and pancreas.

options.text: Vitamin D deficiency causing epithelial metaplasia
options.rationale: Wrong: Vitamin D deficiency affects bone mineralization per lecture, not squamous metaplasia; this would be correct if D deficiency caused epithelial transformation.

options.text: Vitamin E deficiency causing epithelial keratinization
options.rationale: Wrong: Vitamin E deficiency is linked to infertility and lipid abnormalities, not squamous metaplasia; this would be correct if E deficiency produced keratinizing changes.

options.text: Vitamin K deficiency causing mucosal metaplasia
options.rationale: Wrong: Vitamin K deficiency causes coagulopathy per lecture, not metaplasia; this would be correct if K deficiency altered epithelial differentiation.

options.text: Vitamin C deficiency causing squamous transformation
options.rationale: Wrong: Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy and connective tissue problems, not squamous metaplasia as described; this would be correct if collagen defects induced epithelial change.

question: A clinician must decide the next best diagnostic step for a patient with chronic productive cough and suspected bronchiectasis after chest radiograph suggests airway disease. According to the lecture, what is the next best test?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the etiologies, gross findings, and clinical features of bronchiectasis (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Order high resolution computed tomography scan
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture identifies HRCT as the diagnostic gold standard for bronchiectasis and the appropriate next step after suggestive radiography.

options.text: Begin empiric systemic corticosteroid therapy
options.rationale: Wrong: Steroids are not the diagnostic next step; this would be correct only if inflammatory control were the immediate priority over diagnosis.

options.text: Schedule immediate surgical lobectomy evaluation
options.rationale: Wrong: Surgery is reserved for localized disease after diagnosis; this would be correct if focal disease with complications were already confirmed.

options.text: Perform nasal nitric oxide measurement now
options.rationale: Wrong: nNO screens for PCD, not the general next diagnostic step for bronchiectasis; this would be correct if PCD were strongly suspected as the cause.

options.text: Obtain serum alpha one antitrypsin level
options.rationale: Wrong: A1AT testing evaluates a specific etiology but is not the immediate imaging step; this would be correct if clinical suspicion for A1AT deficiency were high.

question: A patient with CF is noted to have hepatic steatosis and biliary cirrhosis. Which bile duct change described in the lecture explains this complication?
cited_learning_objective: Outline the pathogenesis, clinical presentation, and pathologic changes of cystic fibrosis (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Thick viscous bile causing ductal obstruction
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture explains decreased Cl-, Na+, and HCO3- secretion produces thick acidic bile that stagnates, predisposes to infection, and can lead to biliary cirrhosis.

options.text: Autoimmune bile duct destruction with granulomas
options.rationale: Wrong: Autoimmune cholangitis is a different mechanism; this would be correct if immune-mediated bile duct injury were the primary process.

options.text: Cholesterol hypersecretion causing gallstone obstruction
options.rationale: Wrong: Lecture attributes obstruction to thick bile from ion transport defects, not primary cholesterol hypersecretion; this would be correct if gallstones were the main cause.

options.text: Primary sclerosing cholangitis with beading changes
options.rationale: Wrong: PSC is a separate disease entity; this would be correct if cholangiographic beading and inflammatory strictures were present.

options.text: Ischemic bile duct injury from portal hypertension
options.rationale: Wrong: Ischemic injury is not the lecture-described mechanism; this would be correct if vascular compromise caused ductal damage.

question: A 4-year-old with recurrent pneumonia has sweat chloride >60 mmol/L and nasal potential difference more negative than control. Which management step from the lecture addresses pancreatic exocrine insufficiency?
cited_learning_objective: Outline the pathogenesis, clinical presentation, and pathologic changes of cystic fibrosis (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Begin pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture recommends PERT to treat fat and protein malabsorption from pancreatic duct obstruction and exocrine insufficiency in CF.

options.text: Start high dose intravenous corticosteroids
options.rationale: Wrong: Steroids do not correct exocrine pancreatic insufficiency; this would be correct only if autoimmune pancreatitis were the cause.

options.text: Immediate surgical pancreatic resection
options.rationale: Wrong: Resection is not standard for CF-related insufficiency; this would be correct if localized obstructive lesions required removal.

options.text: Administer oral bile acid sequestrants
options.rationale: Wrong: Bile acid sequestrants worsen fat malabsorption; this would be correct only if bile acid diarrhea, not pancreatic insufficiency, were the issue.

options.text: Prescribe long term prophylactic antifungals
options.rationale: Wrong: Antifungals do not treat pancreatic insufficiency; this would be correct if fungal overgrowth in gut were documented causing malabsorption.

question: A patient with suspected bronchiectasis has sputum culture growing a variety of bacteria including Pseudomonas. According to the lecture, which long-term management principle is most appropriate?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the etiologies, gross findings, and clinical features of bronchiectasis (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Chronic and acute targeted antibiotic therapy
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture recommends antibiotic therapy for chronic and acute infections as a cornerstone of bronchiectasis management to control recurrent infections.

options.text: Routine systemic immunosuppression with azathioprine
options.rationale: Wrong: Immunosuppression is not standard and could worsen infections; this would be correct only if an autoimmune etiology required immunomodulation.

options.text: Long term inhaled corticosteroids as monotherapy
options.rationale: Wrong: Inhaled steroids alone do not address infection and mucus clearance; this would be correct if airway inflammation without infection were the dominant problem.

options.text: Immediate bilateral lung transplantation referral
options.rationale: Wrong: Transplant is for end-stage disease, not routine management; this would be correct if irreversible respiratory failure despite therapy were present.

options.text: Daily systemic antifungal prophylaxis indefinitely
options.rationale: Wrong: Antifungal prophylaxis is not standard for bacterial bronchiectasis; this would be correct if fungal colonization were the primary recurrent pathogen.

question: A patient with mild CF symptoms had a negative newborn screen but persistent respiratory complaints. Which diagnostic approach from the lecture is appropriate to detect mild CFTR dysfunction?
cited_learning_objective: Outline the pathogenesis, clinical presentation, and pathologic changes of cystic fibrosis (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Perform nasal transepithelial potential difference testing
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture indicates TEPD is useful when CF is mild and sweat test is inconclusive, detecting increased Na+ absorption and altered potential.

options.text: Repeat newborn immunoreactive trypsinogen measurement
options.rationale: Wrong: IRT is a newborn screen and not diagnostic in older patients; this would be correct only if neonatal screening had been missed and immediate newborn data were needed.

options.text: Order serum anti neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies
options.rationale: Wrong: ANCA testing evaluates vasculitis, not CFTR dysfunction; this would be correct if systemic vasculitis explained pulmonary symptoms.

options.text: Obtain nasal nitric oxide measurement instead
options.rationale: Wrong: nNO screens for PCD, not CF; this would be correct if primary ciliary dyskinesia were the suspected diagnosis.

options.text: Schedule immediate genetic testing for alpha one antitrypsin
options.rationale: Wrong: A1AT testing addresses a different etiology; this would be correct if emphysema from A1AT deficiency were suspected.

question: A patient with CF has recurrent Pseudomonas infections and progressive bronchiectasis. Which long-term advanced therapy mentioned in the lecture may be considered for end-stage pulmonary disease?
cited_learning_objective: Outline the pathogenesis, clinical presentation, and pathologic changes of cystic fibrosis (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Lung transplantation for advanced respiratory failure
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture lists lung transplant as a treatment option in advanced CF when medical therapy fails and respiratory failure progresses.

options.text: Liver transplantation for early biliary cirrhosis
options.rationale: Wrong: While liver disease occurs in CF, the lecture emphasizes lung transplant for end-stage pulmonary disease; liver transplant would be correct if hepatic failure predominated.

options.text: Immediate pancreatic reimplantation surgery
options.rationale: Wrong: Pancreatic reimplantation is not a lecture-described therapy; this would be correct only if a surgical restoration of exocrine function were feasible and indicated.

options.text: Chronic extracorporeal membrane oxygenation indefinitely
options.rationale: Wrong: ECMO is a temporary support, not a long-term solution; this would be correct only as a bridge to transplant in acute decompensation.

options.text: Gene editing therapy routinely available now
options.rationale: Wrong: Gene editing is not presented as an available standard therapy in the lecture; this would be correct if an approved gene therapy existed for CFTR correction.

question: A patient with chronic cough and bronchiectasis is evaluated for underlying causes. Which test from the lecture should be ordered to evaluate for an inherited ciliary disorder?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the pathogenesis and clinical presentation of Kartagener syndrome (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Ciliary ultrastructure analysis from nasal scrape
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture lists nasal scrape with electron microscopy of ciliary ultrastructure as a diagnostic approach for PCD/Kartagener to identify dynein arm defects.

options.text: Serum sweat chloride concentration measurement
options.rationale: Wrong: Sweat chloride diagnoses CF, not PCD; this would be correct if CF were the suspected inherited cause of bronchiectasis.

options.text: Alpha one antitrypsin phenotyping and genotyping
options.rationale: Wrong: A1AT testing evaluates a different inherited cause of lung disease; this would be correct if emphysema from A1AT deficiency were suspected.

options.text: Bronchoscopic biopsy for granulomatous inflammation
options.rationale: Wrong: Biopsy for granulomas targets other etiologies like TB or sarcoidosis; this would be correct if imaging suggested granulomatous disease.

options.text: Sweat sodium chloride fractional excretion test
options.rationale: Wrong: Fractional excretion of sweat sodium is not a standard test for PCD; this would be correct only if a novel sweat metric were validated for ciliary disorders.

question: A patient with CF is noted to have low bone mineral density. Which deficiency described in the lecture most directly contributes to this finding?
cited_learning_objective: Outline the pathogenesis, clinical presentation, and pathologic changes of cystic fibrosis (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Vitamin D deficiency causing decreased bone density
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture links fat malabsorption in CF to deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins including vitamin D, leading to decreased bone mineralization and rickets/osteomalacia.

options.text: Vitamin K deficiency causing osteopenia directly
options.rationale: Wrong: Vitamin K deficiency primarily causes coagulopathy per lecture; this would be correct only if K deficiency were shown to directly reduce bone mineralization in this context.

options.text: Vitamin C deficiency causing bone demineralization
options.rationale: Wrong: Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy and connective tissue problems, not the fat-soluble vitamin-related bone disease emphasized; this would be correct if collagen defects led to bone fragility.

options.text: Excessive vitamin A intake causing bone loss
options.rationale: Wrong: Hypervitaminosis A can affect bone but lecture focuses on deficiency states in CF; this would be correct if documented excessive A intake caused bone issues.

options.text: Isolated iron deficiency anemia reducing bone mass
options.rationale: Wrong: Iron deficiency affects hematopoiesis, not primary bone mineral density as described; this would be correct only if severe anemia indirectly impaired bone health.

question: A patient with suspected CF has recurrent Staphylococcus aureus infections in childhood and later Pseudomonas colonization as an adult. Which lecture point explains this age-related pathogen shift?
cited_learning_objective: Outline the pathogenesis, clinical presentation, and pathologic changes of cystic fibrosis (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Progressive airway damage favors Pseudomonas colonization
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture notes S. aureus in children and Pseudomonas in adults, with chronic airway damage and mucus stasis promoting Pseudomonas over time.

options.text: Age related decline in systemic IgG predisposes adults
options.rationale: Wrong: The lecture attributes pathogen shift to airway environment changes, not systemic IgG decline; this would be correct if humoral immunity waned with age causing the shift.

options.text: Early antibiotic exposure eliminates Pseudomonas in children
options.rationale: Wrong: While antibiotics influence flora, the lecture emphasizes disease progression and environment favoring Pseudomonas; this would be correct if early antibiotics selectively suppressed Pseudomonas long-term.

options.text: Dietary changes in adolescence increase Pseudomonas risk
options.rationale: Wrong: Diet is not implicated in the lecture's pathogen evolution; this would be correct only if specific dietary factors altered airway microbiome favoring Pseudomonas.

options.text: Transition from sweat chloride positivity to negativity
options.rationale: Wrong: Sweat chloride status does not change pathogen profile; this would be correct only if ionic changes over time reversed sweat findings and influenced colonization.

question: A patient with bronchiectasis localized to an obstructed lung segment likely has which underlying mechanism emphasized in the lecture?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the etiologies, gross findings, and clinical features of bronchiectasis (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Focal bronchial obstruction leading to distal dilation
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture explains focal bronchiectasis results from localized obstruction (e.g., tumor, foreign body) causing dilation and infection distal to the blockage.

options.text: Diffuse interstitial fibrosis causing airway dilation
options.rationale: Wrong: Interstitial fibrosis is not the primary cause of bronchiectasis; this would be correct if parenchymal scarring secondarily distorted airways causing dilation.

options.text: Primary vascular malformation compressing bronchi externally
options.rationale: Wrong: External vascular compression is not the typical mechanism; this would be correct if a vascular lesion chronically obstructed a bronchus.

options.text: Systemic autoimmune vasculitis destroying airway cartilage
options.rationale: Wrong: Autoimmune causes can contribute but focal obstruction is the emphasized mechanism; this would be correct if vasculitis directly destroyed bronchial support structures.

options.text: Congenital bronchial cartilage hyperplasia causing dilation
options.rationale: Wrong: Hyperplasia would not typically cause dilation; this would be correct if congenital structural weakness, not hyperplasia, led to dilation.

question: A patient with suspected CF is being counseled about newborn screening. Which biomarker measured in newborn blood is used for initial screening according to the lecture?
cited_learning_objective: Outline the pathogenesis, clinical presentation, and pathologic changes of cystic fibrosis (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Immunoreactive trypsinogen concentration in blood
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture states newborn screening measures IRT, which is elevated in CF due to pancreatic duct obstruction and requires confirmation by sweat testing.

options.text: Serum alpha fetoprotein concentration measurement
options.rationale: Wrong: AFP screens for neural tube defects, not CF; this would be correct if the screening target were fetal neural anomalies.

options.text: Nasal nitric oxide production in neonates
options.rationale: Wrong: nNO is used for PCD screening, not newborn CF screening; this would be correct if PCD screening were the neonatal target.

options.text: Cord blood chloride concentration assay
options.rationale: Wrong: Cord blood chloride is not the standard newborn screen for CF; this would be correct only if sweat chloride could be reliably measured at birth.

options.text: Serum trypsinogen genetic sequencing panel
options.rationale: Wrong: Genetic testing for CFTR can be done but IRT is the standard initial screen; this would be correct if universal genetic newborn screening were the protocol.

question: A patient with CF has recurrent biliary sludge and cholecystitis. Which bile composition change described in the lecture predisposes to these complications?
cited_learning_objective: Outline the pathogenesis, clinical presentation, and pathologic changes of cystic fibrosis (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Decreased bicarbonate and water producing viscous bile
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture explains reduced Cl-, Na+, and HCO3- secretion leads to less water and acidic, viscous bile that stagnates and predisposes to sludge and cholecystitis.

options.text: Excessive bile acid secretion causing detergent injury
options.rationale: Wrong: Excess bile acids are not the lecture mechanism; this would be correct if bile acid hypersecretion caused mucosal damage and stones.

options.text: Autoimmune destruction of intrahepatic bile ducts
options.rationale: Wrong: Autoimmune cholangitis is a different process; this would be correct if immune-mediated ductal injury produced cholestasis and stones.

options.text: Cholesterol hyperabsorption from small intestine
options.rationale: Wrong: Intestinal cholesterol absorption is not emphasized; this would be correct if increased cholesterol saturation of bile caused stone formation.

options.text: Ischemic injury to gallbladder mucosa from hypotension
options.rationale: Wrong: Ischemia is not the typical CF mechanism; this would be correct if acute vascular compromise caused gallbladder inflammation.

question: A patient with chronic cough and clubbing has sputum cultures showing Burkholderia cepacia complex. According to the lecture, this organism is associated with which clinical course in CF patients?
cited_learning_objective: Outline the pathogenesis, clinical presentation, and pathologic changes of cystic fibrosis (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Severe recurrent disease with poor prognosis
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture notes Burkholderia cepacia is associated with severe and recurrent disease in CF and can indicate worse outcomes.

options.text: Benign colonization without clinical significance
options.rationale: Wrong: B. cepacia is clinically significant and linked to severe disease; this would be correct only if the organism were a harmless commensal.

options.text: Typical childhood pathogen causing mild disease
options.rationale: Wrong: S. aureus is more typical in children; this would be correct if the organism were S. aureus rather than B. cepacia.

options.text: Organism responsive to routine topical antiseptics
options.rationale: Wrong: B. cepacia is often resistant and problematic; this would be correct if the organism were easily eradicated with topical measures.

options.text: Indicator of primary ciliary dyskinesia rather than CF
options.rationale: Wrong: B. cepacia is associated with CF severity, not specifically PCD; this would be correct if epidemiology linked it primarily to PCD.
